[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

When you are a mature person and your childhood and carefree days are already over, you have kinda stressful job, you don't feel like playing hard games, or games where you have to concentrate a lot. Sometimes, you just want to come over to your place. make yourself a cup of tea and just relax on comfortable chair and just enjoy some kinda easy game. Preferably, with a mouse only controls.

But to be honest, you need to be ready that games will be strange, or better call them weird or maybe even creepy in some kinda way, cause variety of the titles, that can be played with mouse only is pretty limited and you should expect only chinese visual novels, or some nonsense clickers, or easy tower defense games, or some puzzle logic games.

Or it can be a game like Simulacra. I am not even sure how to call this genre, but what I really do know for sure - this game is completely stupid :) But, in a good funny way. They call it a simulation game, which is kinda fair, but doesn't cover the whole idea of this game. 

So, you start the game playing as not a man, not a woman, just whoever the hell you are, sex is not specified in this game. You found a smartphone and this is where the whole stupid part is about to start. I mean like, imagine you are that person who found a phone, okay? What you gonna do? For me it's completely obvious and easy - if phone is unlockable, you simply need to find someone with a name Mom, Dad, Sister, Boyfriend, Dog in a contact list, call one of them and let them know that you found this device and return it as soon as possible. In case phone is locked, you just need to go to the police station and give it to them for the further actions. Easy as that, don't you think so? But not for our protagonist! Instead all of this, he/she decides to play around with this phone and read messages/mail, check web history, tinder-alike app - I mean like literally everything what you don't have to do, when you find someone's phone, cause this is simply embarassing. For the whole game I had that feeling that I was playing as a retard, who had no job, no personal life, no entertainment sources, literally nothing, so that phone was a greatest relief ever. 

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea.

However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. 

So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you: 

+ Feel like playing some easy game, where is no need for high concentration
+ Are a Black Mirror TV show fan and like all this paranoic idea about how it can be bad somewhere in the future for us with all these high-tech devices
+ Don't agree with me, that carrying a phone to the police station would be the best idea in this situation :)
+ Just looking for a new experience

Avoid this game if you:

- Don't like illogical games, with a stupid protagonist who has no idea what the hell is he doing 
- Have no desire to try something new and unusual

Enjoy!

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones.

A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

I'm surprised. I was expecting something maybe a little hokey or cheesy by the end but what I got was actually a surprisingly effective, creepy tech horror story.

It feels like it wouldn't be out of place as something from the first couple of V/H/S movies. It apes the whole unconventional found footage thing to a tee and despite the occasional spot of grammatical weirdness, it's extremely well made and polished, especially for like five bucks. The acting was reasonably good, the villain was out and out creepy and well done. You can't ask for more, really.

It's about the perfect length for this sort of thing (two to three hours), there's a few puzzles that take some thinking but nothing that's complete and utter nonsense logic and it's replayable and branching with plenty of hidden easter eggs. Kudos to the developers, I'm glad I found out this was a thing.

I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. Dating apps bad. Something about valuing the real world over the virtual. Game certainly doesn't punish you much for becoming a master online troll catfishing manipulator. Wow. That went deeper than I thought. Too bad the villian sucks and I don't care about Anna.

[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a visual novel with some minor horror elements told through a phone.

The basic story is woman goes missing and you end up with her phone. You go through it opening apps, texts, emails, etc, attempting to track her down.

The gameplay is divided into 2 main sections. The first is texting back and forth with people in her text/dating apps. The 2nd section is puzzle based where you need to find/figure out some piece of information to proceed. The game gives you little hints in what you should currently be looking for.

On the plus side: There's some branching paths in response choices that can lead to amusing things happening with various characters. It has multiple endings. Puzzles are actually fairly decent. There're some easter eggs/other things you can mess around with and be amused by.

Looking at the downsides of this: Once you have the whole picture of what's going on, the plot and parts of the story don't make much sense in how they would've play out. The characters aren't that good and one of them is written to be unlikable. Occasionally you'll get video messages and the acting certainly isn't good. Occasional misspellings or responses that don't make much sense. The horror element is more of a background thing, so don't expect it to stand out and be prevalent throughout.

Overall, it's a decent visual novel with some options to fool around with. It's not exceptional in any way, but it's different than standard VRs and has some actual gameplay elements to it, which is nice.

https://youtu.be/glveJEYQO9M?t=792

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.

Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.

review_text_raw:
I must admit. I really REALLY enjoyed playing this game.

When I first saw the tag 'Horror', I was a little scared to play this. I'm not a fan of things that scare me, but I managed to get through this and had a blast. *There are a couple jumpscares obviously because why not XD* (I legit flip out at them and tell them to screw off haha)

So in short, Simulacra is about a girl named Anna who has gone missing, and you have to dig through information through her apps, photos, friends, and even people outside of her circle, in order to find out what the hell happened to her.

And I mean you have to dig through a lot of information sometimes.

However, it's not to say that it wasn't fun doing a treasure hunt. Whenever I figured out how to solve one of the tasks based on the information found in different apps, I felt overjoyed. This game makes you really look for the clues where it makes sense.

Also, by the end of the game, I almost felt like I knew the characters. They were very believable, and that's what really connected with me.

Overall, I just love the idea of using solely a phone. It creates a constraint, allowing for so many possibilities and new ways to create and solve puzzles.

I can say that I have only a couple complaints though.

1) When you look through Anna's message history, you come upon these special messages that are in complete disarray. In order to understand what it said, you had to rearrange the words to fix the message. Sometimes, it was just really difficult for me to figure out what that sentence was. I sometimes maybe spent a little too much time and couldn't progress until I figured it out. Most of the messages weren't important enough to do this, except for one. To be honest, I'm probably just not very good at it.

I only really decrypted those messages for my own curiosity, but because they weren't extremely important except for the story-important ones, there was no huge incentive to decode them.

2) While I do like treasure hunting for those sweet juicy clues in the phone data, sometimes the hints are a little too subtle. I'm not extremely great at puzzle games, so I'll miss details, whether they are obvious or not. I think I took a break because I spent so much time trying to figure out something that was so obvious because I simply missed the detail in a sea of texts. Not a big issue, but I just wanted to point that out for the average gamer playing this. I mean I had to look up something once, so it's not bad on my end.

All in all, this game was just amazing, and I look forward to see what's next :D

(Seriously though. I recommend playing this without any spoilers. This was an amazing experience, and it was a good price for such a wonderful story)

review_text_raw:
Love this game. In the same vein as films like 'Searching', you spend all of your time navigating a device (in this case a phone) in search of a missing person. Simulacra has more a horror tone than 'Searching', but for much of the game's runtime it's only lightly scary, with most of the suspense coming not from supernatural frights but from further unraveling the mystery by feeling like an amateur cybersleuth. 

There are definitely moments where it was frustrating trying to figure out where to go next, but the game generally does a good job of pointing you in the right direction through the use of hints given by the characters in the game. It all feels organic and never too forced. Multiple playthroughs will be needed to see all of the endings, but even just one playthrough will give every player a satisfying experience in the end. 

My few gripes with this game are that the actors aren't really that great in their performances, and for a game that I think is set in the US (at least that seems like the accent everyone is going for), the actor's accents waver quite often. This is obviously not a big budget production, so it's understandable that top shelf talent isn't within reach, but I would say that instead of trying to force a setting, just go with what's available around you. I don't feel that the US setting is necessary to tell this kind of story. I'd also like if there were some way to expedite replays of the game. Yes, if you do a second playthrough you can skip text much more quickly, but I'm thinking of something kinda like Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. In that title there was a branching path menu you could pull up and jump exactly to the point where the story diverged. That would save so much time replaying up until the point where a critical decision was made. 

Conclusion:

Fun cyberdetective game told through a smartphone. Elements of horror, but nothing too overdone so that non-horror fans couldn't enjoy. Gameplay makes you do a fair amount of thinking, without too much handholding, so you feel a sense of accomplishment when you unearth another clue. Tons of easter eggs are there for those willing to look. Performances are not great here, but the voiced parts are minimal and don't interrupt the flow too often. 

Playtime: 4.4 hrs
100% completion

So... this is one of those game I already watched someone (Jacksepticeye) play it, but 7 years is a long time and I forgot the fun little details.

Cons
-Oml, Greg and Cassie's voice actors... that was rough listening to. Taylor's cringe shower serenade tipped into a con for me.

--Just having picture and word puzzles is a bit weird for a horror game like this... but without it, it isn't really a game, I guess.
-Someone needs to check on Ashley, she is always drunk texting Anna...
-Anna is wearing the same thing in each of her vlogs... lol.
--Speaking of, boom mic appearance in one of those vlogs, and a man that isn't one of the actors as well in the vlogs.
-I'm fine with all the horror ambiance... but seriously... knocking?! I could understand for one certain scene, but those knocking cues makes me pause the game and make sure no one is knocking like a maniac on my office. The subtle knocks are worse than the banging knocking.
-Ofc one of the photos is Anna in a towel, lol.
-The most unbelievable thing? Even in 2017, a phone with only 6 apps, 3 of which are e-mail, text, and phone, is completely mystifying, lol. The other three are Internet, Tinder, and Twitter.

[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

A decent enough experience!
The story revolves around the player who receives a phone by a missing girl by the name of Anna and you  must figure out where she went missing and save her while also figuring out about what is causing the many disappearances that have been happening on a dating app. The characters in this game are really cringy and can be hard to enjoy or even have a connection with. The story itself is alright as it does help carry the game along, but its nothing special. 
There really isn't a setting as it takes place all on a phone but its a pretty unique scenario for the player to be put in. 
The visuals are fine as it is all just meant to be a smart phone, but it does look really clean and is convincing enough to feel like a smart phone. 
Sound and audio are again fine as there is really only one bit of soundtrack when opening the game which is a pretty nice piece. The audio is a hit and miss as the audio that is used when the player makes interactions with the phone are good but the background noise that is meant to scare the player does a really poor job at that as it will get to a point where the player would have heard them enough to have no reaction towards it which is disappointing.
The gameplay is fairly simple as all you do is either select different dialog choices, do mini puzzles to load back information and finding clues to move on in the story. Gameplay is decent enough as the story that it intertwines with help it feel more satisfying to do. Finally, i do like the fact that there are multiple endings and outcomes that you experience through the game which would give it more replay-ability
Overall, Simulacra does has a few flaws but if you looking for a decent, unique experience to kill a few hours with i would definitely recommend this.

Yooooo this game is cool!  Simulacra is my first Kaigan game, so if it cribs from any other games they've made, I wouldn't know yet (I've seen reviews saying this game is similar to others, but I'm fresh to the series/catalog..)  

In my first play-through, I failed hard.. Without spoiling too much, let it suffice to say I didn't save the people I was supposed to save.

Some positives:  The choices in the game actually have some bearing on the outcome of the game.  In my first play-through, I chose to be snarky/sarcastic at times.  My snark made me laugh at the time, but came back to bite me in the end.

I find myself _wanting_ to play again, so I can make better decisions.

Some slight negatives: The acting is a wee bit corny at times, but overall, mostly well-done.  Also, the conversation feels a bit "forced" sometimes.  That happens with games like this -- basically, sometimes, it feels like, no matter what you say, the response you get is the same..  I understand that that's a consequence of having to wrap dialog up, but sometimes the progression can be jarring.  Still, it's only a minor issue. 

To me, this game is not very scary (but I have a pretty high horror threshold, so take what I say with a grain of salt.. I watched the original "It" when I was 7 years old.. then I leaned into the whole horror movie/horror game thing..  I watch horror movies alone, in the dark.. So.. yeah..)

Still, overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  I found the presentation (playing the entire game via the interface of someone else's phone) to be interesting, and I want to play again and figure out how to get more positive endings than the one I got the first time around.

review_text_raw:
In Simulacra you find yourself in possession of a stranger's (Anna) phone, who seems to have come to some harm. Through interactions with her phone via video logs, old chat messages, pictures, etc, you gain access to Anna's backstory. Going forward, primarily through "live" chats with Anna's acquaintances, and interactions with some of the other apps on the phone, you unravel the story.

Pros:
[list]
[*] The story progression as implemented through the interactions with the phone apps is OK.
[*] The real-life acting done by Anna and Taylor was good.
[*] The concept of this experience was novel (at least to me).
[/list]

YMMV:
[list]
[*] There are different endings possible, as a function of your choices. I typically don't like this choose-your-adventure type of feature, as it turns into a "guess what the dev" wants me to say sort of thing. Also, this game is nowhere near interesting enough to warrant a second play through, so you are stuck with whatever ending your seemingly random choices yield. For me, this was the "bad" (maybe even super bad?) ending, which left a bad taste in my mouth, and made me feel as though I had wasted my time.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*] The two oft repeated mini-games aren't really fun, and seem shoe-horned in, in an effort to somehow make this more into a game. It doesn't really work. I would classify this as an "experience" more than a "game".
[*] The story itself was underwhelming. 
[/list]

Conclusion: Read the reviews carefully before purchasing this one and get it on sale. It may be a mildly amusing way to pass several hours, but it certainly isn't for everyone. Giving a weak-thumbs up due to binary rating system.

Overall: 5.0/10

Just finished my first playthrough and I can say I really liked the game and I think it totally worth the full price. The premise is original and simple (in a good way): check out an apparently missing person phone's and try to figure out what has happened to her.

In gameplay terms this translates to a visual novel+puzzle solving mash-up. Not that I considerer this a bad thing at all, quite the opossite I think it allows to put emphasis on a strong branching narrative.

I found it easy to "put myself in character" since the game revolves around interacting with the phone's apps and the story tackles on some contemporary problems -like whom you can trust on a social network, how much of info you should share, sexual harrasment, etc-. I know is not the first game that deals with many of these issues: I can recall Orwell but in that case the tone is more scify/conspiracy theory while here's more intimate and gradually turns to horror.
Since I don't want to spoil anything of the story all I'm saying is that the first playthrough took me almost four hours, horror elements are introduced without overdoing it (although some people may argue that they're kinda jump scares if the game hooks you like it happened to me it can be unsettling) and I think it's worth at least a second playthrough to get a different ending.

[i]Go for it if:[/i]
[list]
[*] you're into psychological horror
[*] you have no problem reading "a lot"
[*] you're curious about how text-adventures could evolve
[/list]

[i]Stay away if:[/i]
[list]
[*] you expect a survival horror or an action oriented horror themed game
[*] you're exclusively into complex mechanics/systems
[/list]

It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a "found phone" psychological mystery / horror game where your curiosity has gotten you involved with a mystery... You found this phone on your doorstep. You initially have no idea what to enter, then the phone glitched and revealed its passcode. You find chat logs, call logs, and the owner was Anna. There was a corrupted video where a terrified Anna screamed that don't come after her... Then the message was cut off. 

As you scan the phone's various steps for clues, and maybe even engage in some social engineering with Anna's friends, including (ex-?) boyfriend Greg, bestie Ashley, and dating app date Taylor, you need to reconstruct Anna's life before she went missing, to have a chance at finding out what happened to her...  

The videos are very high quality, but the simulated phone calls don't sound nearly as good. 

The special effects where the phone glitched got the definitely horror feel to it. Same with the time-warp feel when the phone really glitches out. 

The puzzles such as the sentence scramble and photo scramble doesn't quite fit into the gameplay though.  The "sentence scramble" feels a bit of "make work". Same with the photo scramble. 

There seems to be a lot of alternative paths one can take, so there would be a lot of additional achievements should you want a replay or two. 

All puzzles have clues accessible within the phone itself, though some may be more obscure than others. Part of the fun is to figure out the rest. And there are a lot of red herrings. 

All in all, interesting mechanic for a puzzle game and gradual revelation, if you dig this sort of game.

You’re scrolling through messages, watching videos, checking social media, and uncovering clues while trying to figure out what happened. As the story progresses, things become increasingly disturbing, and there were multiple moments that genuinely made me uncomfortable in the best possible way. The game does an excellent job building tension and mystery, making it hard to put down once you start uncovering the truth. The live-action performances help sell the story, and the feeling that something is constantly watching or manipulating events keeps you on edge throughout the entire experience. Overall, SIMULACRA is an amazing horror game that delivers both great scares and an engaging mystery. If you’re looking for a horror experience that feels different from the usual formula, I highly recommend it. Rating: 9/10 A genuinely creepy and immersive horror game that had me hooked from beginning to end and scared me more than I expected.

review_text_raw: An intriguing phone investigation game with a rather unexpected ending! Compared to some other games of this genre most of the puzzles in this one are rather logical and even easy to solve, which at least I like more than riddles so cryptic you have no idea where to even start with them. (There is some extra content locked behind crazier puzzles, but that is more of an easter egg than anything else.) The characters are rather fun and the mystery interesting all the way through! The way to get to the only even somewhat good ending isn't completely to my liking though, as it requires some very precise actions you would pretty much surely fail to pick if you weren't using a guide to help you. But because there's plenty of content to explore outside of that one route, I am still going to give my recommendations to this game.
